claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a reported hierarchical heterostructure featuring multilevel chemical fluctuations and phase boundaries.
High-resolution SEM/TEM images paired with experimental tensile and fracture data can be used to train a surrogate model for HfNbTiVAl10.
Controlled manufacturing parameters can reliably reproduce the characteristic hierarchical heterostructure.
Multiscale chemical fluctuations and interphase boundaries mediate stress distribution in the alloy.
Multiscale chemical fluctuations and interphase boundaries mediate microcrack nucleation.
Multiscale chemical fluctuations and interphase boundaries influence deformation mechanisms.
An image-based ML model can extract microstructural features associated with stress-concentration sites.
An image-based ML model can learn relationships between microstructural features and defect-interaction mechanisms from a modest number of experiments.
The learned microstructure-property relationships can predict Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness.
Using the surrogate avoids full-scale first-principles calculations and extensive CALPHAD evaluations.
Avoiding those calculations will lower computational cost and accelerate prediction.
The proposed method will improve predictive accuracy by approximately 15–20% over traditional approaches.
The proposed method will reduce computational demands by approximately one order of magnitude.
Thermophysical-parameter calculations, CALPHAD, first-principles calculations, and machine learning require high computational resources when combined.
Traditional approaches struggle particularly with accurate prediction of fracture toughness.
The method may become unreliable when sample microstructures deviate substantially from the training distribution.
The method may become unreliable when unforeseen defect mechanisms dominate under extreme loading.
Image-based property prediction has achieved analogous successes elsewhere in materials science.
Prediction gains will depend on image resolution, training-data quality, and processing-induced microstructural variability.
